week.summary: The evidence for the week leaned modestly bearish. Brent fell from 91.70 to 88.63 dollars a barrel between 17 and 20 November (about 3.3%) and is heading for a third weekly loss. The confirmed bearish items were the IEA's 1.7 million bpd Q4 surplus, two consecutive US crude and gasoline builds (API +5.28 million barrels, EIA +3.38 million), a hawkish Fed with the dollar at a 19-month high, and Gulf exports recovering toward pre-war levels. The confirmed bullish items were real but mostly did not remove barrels: the ADNOC vessel attack, US strikes on Qeshm, Houthi gains near Bab el-Mandeb and missile strikes on Riyadh that hit non-oil targets. Iranian mine claims were unconfirmed and carried little weight. Confidence is medium rather than high because the sample is four briefings and the Brent series appears to mix contract months.

bullish_drivers.driver: Confirmed Hormuz tanker attacks, including the ADNOC vessel hit with one crew member missing, and US strikes on the IRGC site on Qeshm
Houthi control of the Bab el-Mandeb coast, an advance towards Aden, and missile strikes on Riyadh (PIF Tower damaged, confirmed on 20 November)
Backwardation widening in the Brent January-February spread ($2.45, $2.64, then $2.81) and speculative length at about the 12th percentile of three years, leaving room for short-covering
Hormuz throughput described as fragile (ANZ: about 49% of pre-war), and the weekend risk of a US or Israeli move on Iran
Iranian claims of further tankers hit by mines (unconfirmed, so low weight)

bearish_drivers.driver: IEA November report: Q4 2026 surplus of 1.7 million bpd and a 2027 surplus of 3.8 million bpd; Gulf exports recovering

API crude build of 5.28 million barrels and gasoline build of 5.12 million barrels, followed by an EIA crude build of 3.38 million barrels and gasoline build of 5.19 million barrels; WTI export arbitrage to Asia and Europe shut
Hawkish FOMC minutes, dollar at a 19-month high, and by 20 November an equity rout with a December Fed hike treated as near certain (reported)
Goldman expects Brent to average $88 in 2027 on a return to surplus; OPEC output back near pre-war levels on a Saudi rebound
De-escalatory signals: Iran's two-day Hormuz plan backed by a regional bloc, Vance ruling out a 'forever war', and Trump reported in no rush to strike Iran (reported)

week.narrative_shift: The week opened as a contest between a surplus narrative and a run of Hormuz attacks, with the market choosing the surplus. On 18 and 19 November inventory builds became the lead bearish argument, while the Shenzhen summit was the main swing event. By 20 November the dominant bearish driver was macro (equities, the dollar, the Fed), and the geopolitical focus had moved from Hormuz mines to Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia. Persistent themes were light positioning, backwardation, the unverified status of Iranian claims, and the 29 November OPEC+ framework as the next scheduled catalyst. Reliance on unconfirmed Iranian mine reports faded as the week went on, since the market kept declining to price them.
week.price_vs_evidence: Prices moved in line with the net evidence. Brent fell about 3.3% over the period and WTI reached its lowest since August. Confirmed escalation did not lift prices because it did not cut flows: the Houthi strikes hit non-oil targets and Hormuz volumes were reported to be recovering. Light positioning and backwardation argue that a premium was not heavily built, so the downside was driven by balance and macro evidence rather than by premium unwinding. The daily moves should be read with care. The 18 November briefing flagged a contract mismatch in the supplied data, and the 19 November headline put front-month Brent near $92 against a recorded 89.82. The 18 November scorecard miss (price up 1.27%) and the size of the daily moves may therefore partly reflect the series rather than the market.
key_risks: A confirmed supply loss, such as a verified mine strike that halts Hormuz flows or a hit on Gulf export infrastructure
A US or Israeli strike on Iran over the weekend, or an Iranian test of the US blockade with an export cargo
Escalating Houthi attacks that move from non-oil targets to Saudi oil facilities or Red Sea shipping
Short-covering from speculative length at about the 12th percentile, with OVX near 50 producing sharp two-way gaps
A relief rally in equities or a softer dollar that removes the macro pressure
week.what_would_change_it: A verified loss of Gulf or Hormuz barrels, or a strike on Iran, would flip the view to bullish. A weaker dollar with a US crude draw would move it to neutral. On the downside, a break below the $87 to $88 technical support cited on 19 November would confirm the bearish view. A rebound towards $96, the bull case in the 19 November scenario table, would show that the premium is being rebuilt.

month.summary: No briefings were supplied for days 8 to 31, so the monthly view rests on the same four briefings as the weekly view and adds no independent evidence. The only longer-run context comes from within those briefings: Brent had already fallen about 18% in 30 days by 18 November, and the 19 November briefing cited a roughly 6% fall over seven days. The balance of evidence was bearish: a projected Q4 surplus, inventory builds, recovering Gulf exports and a tightening Fed. The bullish case rested on confirmed attacks around Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb and Riyadh, plus backwardation and light positioning, but these did not demonstrably cut supply. Confidence is low because the sample is thin and the Brent series mixes contract months.

bullish_drivers.driver: Confirmed attacks on shipping and Gulf states (ADNOC vessel, Qeshm strikes, Houthi missiles on Riyadh), with the Houthis holding the Bab el-Mandeb coast
Steep and widening Brent backwardation ($2.45 to $2.81 on the January-February spread) and speculative length at the 12th percentile of three years
Fragile Hormuz recovery (about 49% of pre-war throughput per ANZ) and the US SPR at its lowest since 1982, which reduces buffers
Stale but supportive EIA STEO forecast of about $100 for November and December, well above spot

bearish_drivers.driver: IEA forecast of a 1.7 million bpd Q4 surplus and 3.8 million bpd in 2027; Goldman sees Brent at $88 on average in 2027, easing to $78 by end-2027
Consecutive large US crude and gasoline builds, and a shut WTI export arbitrage
Hawkish Fed, dollar at a 19-month high and risk-off equities
OPEC output and Gulf exports recovering toward pre-war levels

month.narrative_shift: With only four briefings in the window, any shift is confined to the final week. The market moved from pricing a supply shock to pricing a surplus, and the emphasis moved from tanker attacks to inventories and then to macro. The 29 November OPEC+ ministerial on the 2027 framework is the common forward catalyst across the briefings. No earlier-month narrative is available to compare against.
month.price_vs_evidence: The decline in Brent matches the bearish balance evidence, and the earlier fall of about 18% in 30 days shows the market has been discounting the surplus thesis for some time. Confirmed geopolitical events have not stopped the slide because they did not reduce flows. The market is nonetheless backwardated with light positioning, so the price may be vulnerable to sharp rebounds. Contract-month mixing in the data makes the exact size of the monthly move uncertain.
key_risks: A verified disruption to Hormuz, Red Sea or Saudi export infrastructure
An OPEC+ decision on 29 November that cuts 2027 output or disappoints surplus expectations
A US or Israeli military move against Iran, or a successful Iranian export run through the blockade
A shift in Fed expectations that weakens the dollar and lifts risk assets
Further Ukrainian strikes that change Russian product and crude export flows
month.what_would_change_it: A confirmed fall in Gulf export volumes, or a hawkish OPEC+ outcome on 29 November, would turn the view bullish. Evidence that Hormuz flows have fully normalised alongside continued US stock builds would deepen the bearish case. A weekly close below $87 would confirm further downside, while sustained trade above $96 would point to a rebuilt premium.
